title: Survival prediction of glioblastoma patients using machine learning and deep learning: a systematic review
abstract: Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM), classified as a grade IV glioma by the World Health Organization (WHO), is a prevalent and notably aggressive form of brain tumor derived from glial cells. It stands as one of the most severe forms of primary brain cancer in humans. The median survival time of GBM patients is only 12–15 months, making it the most lethal type of brain tumor. Every year, about 200,000 people worldwide succumb to this disease. GBM is also highly heterogeneous, meaning that its characteristics and behavior vary widely among different patients. This leads to different outcomes and survival times for each individual. Predicting the survival of GBM patients accurately can have multiple benefits. It can enable optimal and personalized treatment planning based on the patient's condition and prognosis. It can also support the patients and their families to cope with the possible outcomes and make informed decisions about their care and quality of life. Furthermore, it can assist the researchers and scientists to discover the most relevant biomarkers, features, and mechanisms of the disease and to design more effective and personalized therapies. Artificial intelligence methods, such as machine learning and deep learning, have been widely applied to survival prediction in various fields, such as breast cancer, lung cancer, gastric cancer, cervical cancer, liver cancer, prostate cancer, and covid 19. This systematic review summarizes the current state-of-the-art methods for predicting glioblastoma survival using different types of input data, such as clinical features, molecular markers, imaging features, radiomics features, omics data or a combination of them. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched databases from 2015 to 2024, reviewing 107 articles meeting our criteria. We analyzed the data sources, methods, performance metrics and outcomes of the studies. We found that random forest was the most popular method, and a combination of radiomics and clinical data was the most common input data. sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: A brain tumor is an abnormal tissue mass in which cells grow and multiply uncontrollably. Brain tumors are classified into two categories based on their malignancy and growth rate. The first category is primary, and the second is secondary. Primary brain tumors originate from the brain's tissues or the brain's immediate surroundings. In contrast, secondary tumors have spread (metastasized) from where they first started to another body part [ 1 ]. Gliomas are a kind of primary brain tumor that occur when the glial cells multiply abnormally. Gliomas grow in the brain and can also affect the spinal cord. Gliomas are divided into four grades (I, II, III, and IV) based on the World Health Organization (WHO) classification, and the grade determines the treatment and prognosis. Grade I and II gliomas are called low-grade gliomas (LGG), and Grade III and IV gliomas are called high-grade gliomas (HGG). The LGG group (also known as the benign tumor) has a longer survival rate than the HGG group. The most aggressive type of primary brain tumor is Grade IV glioma, also known as glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) [ 2 ]. Traditional treatment of GBM is surgical resection followed by radiation therapy or chemotherapy. However, GBM is still associated with poor prognosis, and patients' median overall survival remains limited to 12–15 months [ 3 , 4 ]. The inherent heterogeneity of GBM usually causes variations in prognosis, making the overall survival time largely varied across individuals even though the patients have the same tumor grade and receive similar treatments [ 5 , 6 ]. Accurate prediction of prognosis and survival for each patient is crucial for patients and their families and physicians to support personalized treatment, identify who benefits from aggressive or moderate treatment and avoid ineffective treatment. For example, suppose a patient might have a short survival period. In that case, they probably will not be able to benefit from the surgical treatment and is suitable for palliative irradiation or supportive care. The patient can have surgery if he has a good prognosis and is in general condition [ 7 – 9 ]. Survival prediction is usually done from clinical features using statistical methods. However, with the advancement of artificial intelligence methods that include machine learning and deep learning, researchers have been eager to use these methods for survival prediction, which can combine pathology, histology, molecular, imaging, and clinical features. This systematic review aims to compare studies that used machine learning and deep learning techniques for predicting the survival of GBM patients.

sections.heading: Method and materials
sections.text: This section deals with rules, methods and search criteria used to retrieve the research works related to survival analysis of patients with Glioblastoma cancer.

sections.heading: Research questions
sections.text: The study is carried out to find the answers for the research questions listed below: What are the factors affecting the prediction of survival in patients with Glioblastoma cancer? Which machine learning and deep learning models are used in the prediction of survival in patients with Glioblastoma cancer? How effective are learning methods based on accuracy? Which data sets are used in the prediction of survival in patients with Glioblastoma cancer? What types of data are used?

sections.heading: Search strategy
sections.text: An electronic search following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines was used to review the studies. In the first step, Pubmed, Nature, ScienceDirect, Springer, Wiley, MDPI, and Google Scholar databases with keywords: "Glioblastoma" and "Deep learning" and "Machine learning" and "Survival prediction" in the period January 1, 2015 to October 3, 2024 to retrieve articles those carried out the work related to predicting the survival of patients with glioblastoma cancer using machine learning or deep learning are queried. sections.heading: Medical background
sections.text: GBM is a very aggressive form of brain cancer because it grows quickly, does not respond well to treatment, and has a low survival rate. The current treatment involves removing the tumor surgically if possible, then giving radiotherapy along with temozolomide (TMZ) regimen; however, the tumor often comes back and becomes resistant/adapted to the treatment. The bad prognosis is related to many factors such as tumor diversity, weak immune response, invasion of the tumor into "normal" tissue, production of cancer stem cells, and the fast adaptation of the tumor to harsh treatment [ 10 ]. Survival analysis is a popular topic in clinical research. Survival analysis is a branch of statistics that aims to estimate the time until an event of interest happens, giving the probability of the event happening at each time point. Therefore, several concepts related to the survival chance of a cancer patient are often used when a prognosis is given. Some of them are: The risk of recurrence (e.g., local recurrence or distant metastasis), which is the chance that a treated cancer will come back, Cancer-specific survival (CSS), defined as the time from the diagnosis until death because of a specific type of cancer, Progression-free survival (PFS), defined as the time after treatment when the disease, which could not be removed, does not get worse, Diseasefree survival (DFS), which is the time after the disease is removed when no disease can be found and Overall survival (OS), defined as the time from diagnosis to death or last follow-up, with no limitation on the cause of death [ 11 ] . In current clinical practice, clinicians usually estimate the survival, based on their experience, by looking at the images and taking into account other clinical factors such as age, gender. However, researches show that these judgments and estimates are too biased and optimistic [ 12 ]. Recent studies aim to provide better survival estimates based on multiple types of data such as clinical, molecular, and imaging data. A combination of multiple types of data may give a more detailed description of the underlying characteristics that affect survival and their relationships than single methods. For this purpose, clinical data (such as age, sex, histological grade, stage, etc.) and molecular data (such as mutation status of relevant genes, expression of proteins determined by IHC, etc.), omics data (such as genomics, epigenomics, transcription, proteomics, etc.) and imaging data (such as histological images, magnetic resonance images, computed tomography scans) are used [ 11 ].

sections.heading: Computational approaches
sections.text: Survival prediction is a challenging task that requires the integration of multiple data sources to capture the complexity and heterogeneity of the disease. Traditional statistical approaches, such as the Cox proportional hazards model [ 13 ] and Kaplan–Meier [ 14 ] estimator, often prove inadequate for accurately predicting survival outcomes. These methods struggle when applied to high-dimensional, non-linear, and noisy datasets, particularly those derived from imaging and multi-omics data. As a result, there is a growing need for advanced computational methods that leverage artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, including machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), to improve the accuracy and reliability of survival prediction models. Artificial Intelligence involves using computer systems to simulate human intelligence by analyzing data and applying rules to make predictions. Machine Learning, as a branch of AI, uses data to improve performance across various tasks. Deep Learning, a subset of ML, is based on artificial neural networks with multiple layers, allowing it to process complex patterns in data. These techniques are applied to patient data to develop models that predict outcomes like survival. Data collected from large-scale institutional and registry sources—ranging from clinical records to imaging datasets—are often used to train these algorithms, enhancing their accuracy in predicting survival outcomes [ 15 ].

sections.heading: Categorization of survival prediction models
sections.text: The following is a systematic categorization and summary of existing survival prediction models based on statistical, machine learning, and deep learning methods. Statistical models: Research status: Statistical models, including the Cox proportional hazards model and the Kaplan-Meier estimator, are traditional approaches commonly used for survival analysis. These models are valuable for their interpretability and simplicity, especially in smaller or homogeneous datasets. Advantages: These models offer a straightforward interpretation of survival probabilities and hazard ratios, which are clinically useful. They can also work well with limited data and require relatively simple computation. Limitations: Statistical models face notable limitations, such as difficulty in managing non-linear relationships and high-dimensional data. They depend on assumptions like proportional hazards, which may not hold true in complex real-world datasets. Furthermore, these models have difficulty in integrating diverse data modalities, such as imaging and molecular features, which are increasingly critical in modern survival prediction [ 15 ]. Machine learning models: Research status: ML algorithms like Support Vector Machines (SVM) [ 16 ], Random Forests (RF) [ 17 ], and Gradient Boosting [ 18 ] have gained popularity in survival prediction due to their flexibility and capacity to handle a wide range of data types. These models can accommodate non-linear relationships, making them suitable for clinical data, imaging, and genomic features. Advantages: ML models can integrate various data types, such as clinical, radiomic, histological, and molecular features. Their ability to handle complex interactions and capture non-linearities allows them to generate more accurate prognostic models. Limitations: Despite their strengths, ML models can be prone to overfitting, particularly with small or unbalanced datasets. Additionally, these models are often less interpretable than statistical models, making it difficult to extract clinically relevant insights. Furthermore, handling missing data and effectively integrating multi-modal datasets, such as clinical, imaging, and molecular data, remain significant challenges, often requiring advanced preprocessing methods [ 15 ]. Deep learning models: Research status: DL models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [ 19 ], Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [ 20 ], and more recently, Transformer-based models, have shown significant promise in survival analysis. These models are particularly useful when working with high-dimensional and complex data like medical imaging, genomic profiles, and multi-modal clinical data. Advantages: DL models are capable of learning intricate patterns and relationships within the data, reducing the need for manual feature engineering. They can seamlessly integrate multiple data modalities (e.g., imaging, genomic, clinical) and leverage the information for accurate survival predictions. Limitations: However, DL models require a significant amount of training data, which may not always be available, especially in rare cancer cases. They are computationally intensive and susceptible to overfitting when applied to small datasets. Additionally, their "black-box" nature presents challenges in interpretability, complicating clinical application. To address this, research is focusing on developing explainability methods (e.g., SHAP 1 [ 21 ] , LIME 2 [ 22 ] ) to provide more transparency [ 15 , 23 ].

sections.heading: Survival prediction as a regression or classification task
sections.text: Survival time prediction can be approached as either a regression or a classification problem, depending on the task and data type: Regression: In regression-based survival prediction, the objective is to estimate a continuous outcome, such as the number of days or months a patient is expected to survive. This approach is suitable when accurate time-to-event data is available. Classification: Classification models, on the other hand, predict discrete categories, such as survival status (alive or deceased) or survival groups (e.g., short-term, medium-term, or long-term). This method is often used when the goal is to categorize patients into risk groups for targeted treatments [ 15 , 24 ]. BraTS also focuses on predicting overall patient survival. BraTS utilizes multi-institutional pre-operative MRI scans of glioma patients with pathologically confirmed diagnoses and available molecular markers.

sections.heading: Challenges and limitations in survival prediction models
sections.text: Despite the advancements in survival prediction models, several significant limitations remain that must be addressed to enhance their accuracy and clinical utility. These limitations span multiple dimensions, including data availability, model complexity, data heterogeneity, and transparency issues. Below is a detailed overview of these challenges

sections.heading: Data sufficiency
sections.text: Although efforts have been made to collect and share extensive cancer-related data with the scientific community, the quantity of available data remains insufficient. Most cancer datasets contain hundreds of observations, which is considerably less than datasets from other fields that typically include tens of thousands of samples. This limitation makes it difficult to capture the complexity and variability of the disease accurately, hindering the development of robust models that produce reliable results. Increasing the sample size, particularly for underrepresented cancer types, could significantly enhance the performance of survival prediction models [ 128 ].

sections.heading: Limited availability of public multimodal datasets
sections.text: Access to multimodal datasets is often restricted, as many existing datasets are maintained privately by hospitals or research centers due to data privacy laws. This lack of publicly accessible multimodal data, which combines imaging, clinical, and genomic information, limits researchers' ability to develop and validate comprehensive models. Changes in data privacy regulations, along with the implementation of encryption and privacy-preserving methods, are essential to support predictive analysis on private databases without compromising patient confidentiality [ 129 ].

sections.heading: The "Black Box" problem in AI models
sections.text: One of the critical challenges in adopting AI systems in healthcare is the lack of transparency and interpretability, often referred to as the "black box" problem. Clinicians need to understand how AI models make their predictions to trust and use them confidently, especially in critical situations where patient lives are at stake Although Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods, such as SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations), aim to make these models more interpretable, their effectiveness in practice is still debated. Furthermore, there is a lack of standardized metrics to evaluate the quality of explanations provided by these models, suggesting that while XAI shows promise, more development and validation are needed [ 23 ].

sections.heading: Data heterogeneity
sections.text: The variability in clinical datasets presents a major challenge for survival prediction models. This heterogeneity arises from several factors: Variability Among Patients: Datasets often include data from patients with diverse cancer types, stages, and treatment histories. While this diversity can aid in creating more generalizable models, it also introduces significant variability. For instance, a dataset might contain more glioblastoma cases than rarer types like oligodendroglioma, leading to imbalanced data that models may struggle to generalize across. Techniques such as oversampling, undersampling, and synthetic data generation (e.g., SMOTE 3 ) [ 130 ] can be used to address these imbalances. Integration of Multimodal Data: Combining diverse data types (e.g., imaging, genomics, and clinical records) offers a holistic view of patient health but introduces complexity in data integration. Not all patients may have complete data across all modalities, complicating the development of models that can effectively leverage the available information. Advanced methods like multi-view learning or deep learning architectures that can handle missing modalities may be required to address this challenge. Handling Missing Data: Missing data is common in clinical datasets due to incomplete tests or patient dropouts. If not managed properly, this missing information can bias model outcomes. Techniques such as K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) imputation, multiple imputation strategies, or Bayesian models can help manage this issue, but their application needs careful consideration to avoid introducing new biases. Variations in Data Collection Methods: Inconsistencies in data collection methods, such as differences in imaging devices or sequencing platforms, can affect data quality. For example, MRI scans from machines with different magnetic field strengths (e.g., 1.5T vs. 3T) may produce images of varying quality, impacting model performance if these discrepancies are not harmonized. Standardization techniques, such as ComBat for genomic data or intensity normalization for imaging, are essential for ensuring consistency and reliability [ 11 ].

sections.heading: Computational complexity and resource requirements
sections.text: Advanced deep learning models, while effective in capturing complex patterns, require significant computational resources for training and deployment. These resource-intensive requirements may not be feasible in all research settings, particularly in low-resource environments. Additionally, the complexity of these models adds to the challenge of making them accessible and practical for widespread clinical use [ 131 ].

sections.heading: Bias and ethical considerations
sections.text: Bias in datasets and models is another critical issue that can affect the fairness and generalizability of survival prediction models. Existing models may reflect and reinforce biases present in healthcare data, such as demographic disparities or unequal access to healthcare services. Ensuring that models are developed and validated on diverse and representative datasets is crucial to prevent such biases. Moreover, ethical concerns related to the use of sensitive data, particularly genetic and genomic information, must be addressed. Data protection measures, including secure storage and anonymization techniques, are essential for maintaining patient privacy and ensuring the responsible use of AI in healthcare [ 132 ].

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Survival prediction is a key application of computational techniques in healthcare, which aims to improve the quality of care for patients. It is a type of time-to-event prediction, which measures the duration from the start of observation until the occurrence of death (or another specific event) for the patient under observation, or until the end of observation. Survival analysis can help to estimate the risk of death or recurrence for patients based on various types of data, such as clinical, imaging, omics, and environmental data. In the context of cancer survival, survival analysis corresponds to the time between diagnosis and death from the disease, and can help to assess the prognosis and personalized treatment planning for cancer patients. Survival prediction is a difficult task that requires the combination of multiple types of information to capture the diversity and variability of the disease. Traditional statistical methods are not sufficient or suitable to predict survival from imaging, multi-omics, or their integration, as they have limitations in dealing with high-dimensional and non-linear. Therefore, computational approaches that use artificial intelligence techniques, such as machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), have been developed and applied to enhance the precision and robustness of survival prediction models. The results of this systematic review show that machine learning and deep learning methods have been widely applied to survival prediction of glioblastoma patients, using different types of input data, such as clinical features, molecular markers, imaging features, radiomics features, omics data, or a combination of them. This systematic review examines the data sources, methods, performance measures, and results of 107 studies published from 2015 to 2024. Throughout this review, we noticed that: The most frequently used method was random forest, which is a tree-based ensemble learning method that can handle high-dimensional and heterogeneous data. The most prevalent input data was a combination of radiomics and clinical data, which can capture both the tumor phenotype and the patient characteristics, and provide complementary information for survival prediction. Most researchers used Python and R to develop survival prediction models. Among the public datasets, most of the studies has been done using TCGA data.

sections.heading: Future work
sections.text: Exploration of transformer models and new-generation AI techniques: Current Research Landscape: While there are a few studies that have started exploring the application of transformer models for survival prediction, this area is still relatively new and underdeveloped in the context of medical-assisted diagnosis. Recent advancements in AI demonstrate the potential of transformers, particularly in handling complex, multi-modal data integration. Transformer architectures, such as Vision Transformers (ViTs) and other variants, have shown promise in other fields, and their application is beginning to emerge in survival analysis. Proposed Future Direction: Future studies should build on these initial findings and further develop transformer-based models for survival prediction. Given their ability to process sequential and high-dimensional data effectively, transformers have the potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of models that integrate imaging, clinical, and genetic data. Integration of big data, multi-omics, and multi-modality: The Role of Big Data: The next generation of medical-assisted diagnosis models must leverage big data to capture the complexity and diversity of patient populations. This involves incorporating large-scale datasets that encompass patient demographics, clinical records, imaging data, and genetic profiles from multiple institutions and populations. Multi-Omics Data: Integrating diverse omics data (e.g., genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics) can provide deeper insights into the molecular mechanisms driving cancer progression and patient outcomes. Future models should develop strategies to efficiently combine these different data types, using advanced techniques like multi-omics integration frameworks or hierarchical models that account for data at different biological levels. Modality Data: The future of medical diagnosis models lies in effectively merging various data modalities (e.g., MRI, CT scans, histopathological images, clinical data, and omics information) to create a unified predictive model. Developing deep learning architectures, such as hybrid networks that integrate CNNs, RNNs, and transformers, could facilitate the processing and integration of these data types. Large Models: Implementing large-scale models capable of processing and learning from extensive and diverse data is crucial for improving prediction accuracy. Although transfer learning is currently underexplored in survival prediction, it presents an opportunity for future research. Applying transfer learning techniques could help build models that adapt to new data efficiently, especially in scenarios where acquiring large amounts of labeled medical data is challenging. Development of Ethical and Transparent AI Systems: Development of ethical and transparent AI systems: Addressing the "Black Box" Problem: As AI models become more complex, enhancing their interpretability remains critical. Future work should prioritize the development of Explainable AI (XAI) solutions that provide clinicians with transparent and understandable outputs. These models must offer insights into which features or data sources influence predictions, enabling clinicians to make informed decisions confidently. Privacy and Security: With the integration of big data and multi-omics information, ensuring patient privacy and data security is essential. Research should focus on developing privacy-preserving techniques such as federated learning and encrypted data sharing, allowing models to learn from distributed datasets without compromising patient confidentiality. Scalability and generalization: Future research should explore ways to scale these advanced models for global application, ensuring that they generalize across diverse populations and healthcare systems. Collaborations across multiple research centers and hospitals will be necessary to gather and validate multi-center datasets that enhance the models' robustness and applicability.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This article has presented a systematic review of the current state-of-the-art machine learning and deep learning methods for survival prediction of glioblastoma patients. The article has analyzed the data sources, methods, performance metrics, and outcomes of 107 studies published from 2015 to 2024. The article revealed that random forest was the most frequently used method, and combining radio mics and clinical data was the most prevalent input data. Predicting survival with high accuracy can assist personalized clinical decision-making in glioblastoma patients. The scientific domain is shifting towards machine learning and deep learning models built on high-dimensional data, often with promising results. However, these models have yet to be implemented in clinical care. To facilitate the clinical adoption of high-performing machine learning and deep learning models, future efforts should focus on harmonizing data acquisition methods, improving model interpretability, and externally validating these models in a multicentered, prospective way. The article hopes to provide a helpful reference and guidance for researchers and practitioners interested in this topic.
